title: The Enrollment Roller Coaster
author: Aldeman, Chad
summary: Chad Aldeman uses Washington State's unique monthly enrollment tracking system to reveal a consistent within-year enrollment pattern that most states cannot see: K-12 enrollment rises from September to October, then declines steadily through May, losing approximately 1% of students by spring. This year in Washington that amounted to roughly 11,000 fewer students by May than were counted in October. Aldeman argues that because most states use a single fall count to drive annual funding, they are almost certainly funding schools based on enrollment numbers higher than what districts actually serve for most of the school year. The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted overall enrollment levels but did not change the within-year pattern. He draws an analogy to gym design: building a gym for January membership surges rather than March attendance is obviously bad planning, yet this is effectively how most states calibrate staffing and budgets. The piece ends with a call for policymakers to investigate whether their states experience similar within-year declines and what that means for both funding formulas and staffing models.
points: * Washington State's monthly enrollment tracking exposes what single-date fall counts cannot: a consistent pattern where districts lose about 1% of students between October and May -- 11,000 students in the current year alone. * The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted overall enrollment levels but did not change the within-year pattern -- before and after, the same October-to-May decline persisted, suggesting this is structural, not a pandemic-era anomaly. * States relying on a single fall count may be funding schools based on enrollment levels higher than what districts actually serve for most of the year -- a misalignment that compounds staffing and resource miscalculation. * The missing students likely reflect a combination of family mobility, private school and homeschooling transfers, and dropout/re-engagement cycles -- invisible without continuous or periodic re-counting. * Aldeman's gym analogy cuts cleanly: designing a gym for January's membership surge rather than March's actual attendance is exactly what fall-count funding does -- it optimizes for the moment of greatest enrollment, not the reality of the year.
quotes: Every fall, schools count their students for funding purposes. But by the time spring arrives, many of those students are gone. In most states, we don't really have a way to know how enrollment changes across the school year.

The pattern is remarkably consistent. Enrollment rises from September to October and then gradually declines throughout the rest of the school year. By May, districts are serving about 1% fewer students than they reported in October.

The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted overall enrollment levels, but it did not fundamentally change the within-year pattern. Before the pandemic and after it, Washington schools typically lost about 1% of their students between fall and spring.

States that rely on a single fall count date may be funding schools based on enrollment levels that are higher than what districts serve for much of the school year. And the patterns may be smaller than they are in places with only a single fall count.

If policymakers are basing funding and staffing models on October enrollment counts, it's a bit like designing a gym around the surge of new members who show up in January rather than the number who are still attending by spring.
